title: The Storm and the Retreat • Jibril’s Command • Sa‘d’s Judgment • Final Word

blocks.1: When the alliance had begun to break apart from within through mutual distrust, Allah sent a stormy night of fierce cold. Pots overturned, tents were uprooted, fires went out.
blocks.3: I have been helped by the east wind, and ‘Ad were destroyed by the west wind.{{1}}
blocks.4: The same wind, two fates. Destruction for one people, help for another; the wind is only a means, the decision is always Allah’s. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA) used to say,
blocks.6: We were with the Prophet {{1}} on the night of the Confederates; a fierce storm and bitter cold gripped us. The Prophet {{2}} said, is there anyone who will bring me news of the enemy camp, that Allah will make him my companion on the Day of Resurrection? We kept silent, none of us answered. He said again, the same words; again silence. The third time too none of us answered. Then he said, rise, Hudhayfah, bring us news of the enemy camp. After he called me by my name, I had no choice but to rise. He said, go, bring me news, but do not startle them against me. As I went away from him, it felt as if I were walking through a hot bath, until I reached them. I saw Abu Sufyan warming his back at the fire. I set an arrow on the bow and wanted to shoot; but I remembered the words of the Prophet {{3}}, do not startle them; had I shot, it would surely have hit; but I came back, and again it felt as if I were walking through a hot bath.{{4}}
blocks.7: Just then Abu Sufyan stood in the darkness of the night and said, O Quraysh, we cannot hold out here; the horses and camels are dying, Banu Qurayzah too did not keep their word, and this storm has thrown everything of ours into chaos; go back. Then he himself mounted his camel and set off, and the rest slipped away one by one.{{1}}
blocks.8: Hudhayfah (RA) went back and gave the Prophet {{1}} the whole report. As soon as the reporting was over he suddenly felt the cold; the Prophet {{2}} wrapped around him a part of the cloak in which he himself used to pray. He slept until morning. In the morning the Prophet {{3}} called, get up, sleepyhead.{{4}}
blocks.9: Three times he called and no one responded; only after being called by name did one stand up. Fear is human; but when called by name, that same person can walk calmly through the midst of the enemy camp. The Prophet {{1}} used to say afterwards,
blocks.11: There is no god but Allah, alone; He honoured His soldiers, helped His servant, and alone defeated the Confederates; after Him there is nothing.{{1}}
blocks.12: By morning the enemy camp was seen to be empty. Without a sword swung, without an arrow shot, a whole army had slipped away into the darkness of the night. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.14: From now on we will attack them, and they will not attack us; it is we who will march toward them.{{1}}
blocks.15: As soon as a defensive war had ended, the Prophet {{1}} declared, no more defence after this, now it is the turn of attack. After the Trench, Madinah was never attacked in this way again. In this siege of nearly a month only six Companions were martyred on the Muslim side; there is some variation in the narrations about the number of the enemy’s dead.{{2}}
blocks.16: The siege that was won without any sword fighting still had loss of life; war is never entirely without cost, yet the cost of this war was astonishingly low.
blocks.18: After the enemy left, the Prophet {{1}} laid down his weapons and sat down to bathe. Just then Jibril (AS) came.
blocks.20: Have you laid down your weapons? By Allah, we have not laid them down yet. Go out toward them. The Prophet {{1}} asked, where? He pointed toward Banu Qurayzah.{{2}}
blocks.21: The war that had seemed to be over was in fact not yet over. Banu Qurayzah had broken the pact at the Muslims’ most dangerous moment; the reckoning of that betrayal remained. Anas (RA) used to say, I can still seem to see the dust rising in the lane of Banu Ghanm, the dust of Jibril’s army, when the Prophet {{1}} set out toward Banu Qurayzah.{{2}}
blocks.22: The Prophet {{1}} asked for a volunteer to bring news from the enemy camp. al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam (RA) responded. He asked again, al-Zubayr (RA) responded again. The third time too it was the same. The Prophet {{2}} said,
blocks.24: Every prophet has a hawari, a devoted helper; my hawari is al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam.{{1}}
blocks.25: Hudhayfah (RA) had to be called by name, only then did he get up. In al-Zubayr’s (RA) case there was never any need to call; each time he raised his hand first. Fear does not lift in everyone the same way, some need to be called by name, some do not; yet both in the end stepped forward. The Prophet {{1}} announced that no one should pray ‘Asr before reaching Banu Qurayzah. The huge army was then moving strung out along the road, not everyone was in one place together. On the way, the time of ‘Asr came for one group. Some said, we will pray when we get there, as was said; some said, no, he did not mean this, let us pray on the way. The matter did not reach the Prophet {{2}} at that moment, was not settled at that moment; later, when he was informed, he blamed no one.{{3}}
blocks.26: The same command, two kinds of understanding; both sincere, both reasonable. The Prophet {{1}} told no one they were wrong, because the real goal was to arrive quickly, not to follow it letter by letter. When there is honesty in the effort to understand, even a differing view becomes tolerable. On reaching the fortress the Prophet {{2}} told the Companions to hold up shields and stand around him, so that his voice would carry clearly into the fortress. Then he called out, O brothers of monkeys and pigs! Surprised, they replied, O Abu al-Qasim, you never used to speak obscenely.{{3}}
blocks.27: The tribe that broke the pact at the Muslims’ most dangerous moment now has its fortress surrounded; the time has come to settle the reckoning of betrayal.
blocks.29: Before surrendering, Ka‘b ibn Asad, the leader of Banu Qurayzah, laid out three paths to his community. He said, come, let us accept Muhammad; by Allah, it has become clear to you too that he is a true prophet, the one who is written of in your own Book. They said, we will never abandon the law of the Torah. Ka‘b said, then come, let us kill our wives and children with our own hands, then fall upon Muhammad and his companions sword in hand; if we die, we die, leaving no burden behind. They said, kill these helpless people? What is the use of living without them? Ka‘b said, then let us attack tonight, Saturday night; Muhammad will not think that we would do anything on this night. They said, spoil the Sabbath? Have you forgotten what came upon our forefathers? Ka‘b said, from the day you were born from your mothers’ wombs, you have not been firm of purpose for even one night.{{1}}
blocks.30: Ka‘b had admitted with his own mouth that the truth had become clear to them. Yet instead of bowing before that truth, they chose one path of destruction after another, even to killing their own children with their own hands. To know the truth and refuse it out of pride is the greatest loss; the danger that could have been avoided with one acknowledgement became in the end inevitable. In the end they summoned their old ally Abu Lubabah (RA) and asked his advice. Seeing him, the women and children broke into tears. They asked, would it be right to submit to Muhammad’s decision? Abu Lubabah (RA) said yes with his mouth, but with his hand pointed to his throat, indicating that it meant killing. As soon as he had said it, he realised, before his feet had even moved from that place he understood, that he had betrayed Allah and His Messenger. He went to the mosque and tied himself to a pillar, saying, I will not move from here until Allah accepts my repentance.{{1}}
blocks.31: A man, realising his mistake, punished himself, before returning to Allah. This very honesty in admitting a mistake has kept him in history. After a siege of twenty-five days Banu Qurayzah surrendered, on one condition, that they would accept the decision of Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA). Sa‘d (RA) was still bedridden with the wound from the arrow.{{1}}
blocks.33: The people of Banu Qurayzah came down agreeing to Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh’s judgment. The Prophet {{1}} sent for Sa‘d, and he came riding a donkey. When he came near the mosque the Prophet {{2}} said to the Ansar, rise toward your chief, or your best man. Then it was said, these have come down agreeing to your judgment. He said, then I judge that their fighters be killed, and their children be taken captive. The Prophet {{3}} said, you have judged according to the command of Allah; sometimes he used to say, according to the command of the King.{{4}}
blocks.34: A wounded man, brought from his bed, yet both sides placed their trust in his decision. The weight of justice does not depend on bodily strength; it depends on conscience. This judgment coincided with the law of Banu Qurayzah’s own Torah, concerning a hostile tribe. Sa‘d (RA) showed no partiality even against the old allies of his own tribe; he decided on the path of justice.{{1}}
blocks.35: The Qur’an has described this fate of Banu Qurayzah like this,
blocks.37: Those of the People of the Book who had aided them (that is, the enemies of the Muslims), Allah made them come down from their fortresses and cast such fear into their hearts that you were killing some of them and taking some captive. Allah made you heirs to their land, their houses and their wealth, and to a land on which you had not yet set foot. Allah has power over all things.{{1}}
blocks.38: The verse also spoke of the land where no foot had yet been set. About two years after the fall of Banu Qurayzah, Khaybar came into Muslim hands; a promise whose fulfilment had to wait for time. It is hard to believe Allah’s promise exactly when its proof is not yet visible to the eyes; but that very time of waiting is the real test of faith. As soon as the judgment was over, Sa‘d’s (RA) wound began to bleed afresh. Soon after, he attained martyrdom. The Prophet {{1}} himself said that at his death the Throne of Allah shook, the doors of heaven were opened, and seventy thousand angels witnessed his funeral.{{2}}
blocks.39: At the burial the Prophet {{1}} was sitting beside the grave. Suddenly he recited tasbih twice, and everyone recited tasbih with him. Then he said takbir twice, and everyone said takbir. The Companions asked, O Messenger of Allah, what happened? He said,
blocks.41: The grave pressed upon this righteous servant so tightly that Allah later widened it for him.{{1}}
blocks.44: There is a squeezing in the grave; if anyone were to be saved from it, Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh would have been saved.{{1}}
blocks.45: He at whose death the Throne shook, at whose funeral seventy thousand angels bore witness, even his grave was not spared the first blow. Even the person of the greatest rank is not above reckoning; in Allah’s sight the reckoning is the same, the difference lies only in mercy.
blocks.47: From this dars of the fifth year of the Hijrah some pictures remain. A proposal of Salman (RA), which changed even the Arabs’ way of war. Two stones on the belly of the Prophet {{1}}, where the Companions had one each. Jabir’s (RA) one sa‘ of barley and a kid, with which several hundred people were fed. ‘Ali’s (RA) single combat, which gave the army of ten thousand its first shock. Safiyyah’s (RA) courage with a stick in hand, which protected a whole fortress. Nu‘aym’s (RA) three journeys, which broke an alliance of ten thousand without any sword. Sa‘d’s (RA) wounded body, yet one whose decision both sides trusted. And the greatest picture is the Prophet’s {{2}} own, carrying earth himself with a body smeared in mud, the hungriest of all yet first to get to work. So take one deed home from today’s dars.
blocks.49: While digging the trench the Prophet {{1}} tied two stones to his belly out of hunger, where the Companions had tied one each; in the share of hardship he was before everyone, in the share of comfort after everyone. Today I will ask myself a question: do I always make sure of my own share first, or have I ever learned to give others from my own share? Today I will give a little from my own plate of food to someone whom people do not usually ask after; I will not give up this small habit from today.

footnotes.1: Sahih Muslim 1788 (Kitab al-Jihad wa al-Siyar, Bab Ghazwat al-Ahzab; from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA), through Ibrahim al-Taymi ← his father Yazid ibn Sharik).
footnotes.2: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Khandaq’ (Abu Sufyan’s announcement and return). Sirah-based.
footnotes.3: Sahih Muslim 1788 (Kitab al-Jihad wa al-Siyar, Bab Ghazwat al-Ahzab; from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA), through Ibrahim al-Taymi ← his father Yazid ibn Sharik).
footnotes.6: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ‘Shuhada’ Yawm al-Khandaq’ (the list of names of the Muslim martyrs, six). Sirah-based. In different compilations the number of the enemy’s dead appears as various figures between eight and twelve, none taken as final, so no specific number is mentioned in the dars.
footnotes.9: Sahih al-Bukhari 2847 (from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA)). The narrator Sadaqah ibn al-Fadl himself said ‘I think it was the day of the Trench’ (‘azunnuhu yawm al-Khandaq’), that is, the time of the event is not definitely fixed in the original text of the hadith, it is the sub-narrator’s guess. The dars has placed it keeping this uncertainty in mind.
footnotes.10: Sahih al-Bukhari 4119 (from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (RA)). From the two expressions ‘ba‘duhum’ (some of them) and ‘fa-dhukira dhalika li-l-Nabiyy {{1}}’ (the matter was reported to the Prophet {{2}}, in the passive voice, who reported it is unspecified) in the original Arabic text of the hadith it is understood that the matter was not settled in his direct presence, he was informed afterwards. ⚠ The text of the hadith contains no account of troop numbers or who was where; the statement ‘the army was strung out along the road’ in the dars is only a reasonable inference drawn from these two expressions, not a direct statement of the hadith. In the first draft a specific troop number (3,000, which is actually the figure for the opening moment of the Trench, not of this expedition) and an additional assumption that ‘the Prophet {{3}} was in the front group’ had been placed by mistake; they were caught in re-verification and removed.
footnotes.11: ‘Abd al-Razzaq ibn Hammam, al-Musannaf (the incident of standing with shields and the call at the start of the Banu Qurayzah siege). There is real disagreement among muhaddithun about the chain of this narration; some have called it weak, and the words of the reply too have come differently through different sources (in one place ‘lam takun fahhashan’, that is, you were never foul-mouthed, in another ‘ma kunta jahulan’, that is, you never behaved like an ignorant person). In the dars the translation of the first narration (‘lam takun fahhashan’) has been used. There is also discussion among scholars explaining it, since such harsh language may seem contrary to the Prophet’s {{1}} natural gentleness. In the dars it is used only as a scene, not as an independent proof.
footnotes.12: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Fasl fi Ghazwat Banu Qurayzah’ (Ka‘b ibn Asad’s three proposals and their rejection). Sirah-based.
footnotes.13: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Fasl fi Ghazwat Banu Qurayzah’ (the signal of Abu Lubabah ibn ‘Abd al-Mundhir (RA), his tying himself to the pillar of the mosque until his repentance was accepted; the same incident is narrated in close wording through Musa ibn ‘Uqbah and al-Zuhri too, the number of nights he stayed tied differs by narration, 6 or 20 nights). According to Ibn Hisham’s note, through Sufyan ibn ‘Uyaynah ← Isma‘il ibn Abi Khalid ← ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Qatadah, it is reported that Surah al-Anfal 8:27 was revealed on this very occasion; this is a separate chain. Sirah-based.
footnotes.14: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat Banu Qurayzah’ (the siege lasting twenty-five days and the terms of surrender). Sirah-based; there is slight variation among narrations about the number of days of the siege.
footnotes.16: Ma‘arif al-Qur’an, commentary on Surah al-Ahzab verses 26–27 (the discussion of Banu Qurayzah’s ruling being consistent with the Torah); page-number verification pending.
footnotes.17: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 3, Surah al-Ahzab 33:26–27, pp. 76–77 (Taqi ‘Uthmani; checked against the rendered PDF). The phrase ‘about two years later Khaybar’ is a calculation: the fall of Banu Qurayzah was late in the 5th year of the Hijrah (the month of Dhu al-Qa‘dah), the conquest of Khaybar early in the 7th year (the month of Muharram); an interval of about one year and two to three months in between; this figure is not mentioned directly in the verse or hadith.
footnotes.18: Sahih al-Bukhari 3803 (through Jabir (RA), ‘ihtazza ‘arsh al-Rahman li-mawt Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh’); Sahih Muslim 2466 (through Anas (RA), a close narration). The part about the doors of heaven being opened and seventy thousand angels is a separate hadith: Sunan al-Nasa’i (from Ibn ‘Umar (RA), marfu‘), ‘hadha alladhi taharraka lahu al-‘arsh, wa futihat lahu abwab al-sama’, wa shahidahu sab‘una alfan min al-mala’ikah, laqad dumma dammatan thumma furrija ‘anhu’ (This is the one for whom the Throne shook, the doors of heaven were opened, seventy thousand angels witnessed; he was squeezed once, then released from it). Imam al-Albani (may Allah have mercy on him) called this hadith sahih, and included it in both Sahih Sunan al-Nasa’i and Sahih al-Jami‘. Added on 30 September 2026 at the user’s request; at first, because an AI summary from a web search did not clearly give this narration’s source book and grading, it was temporarily omitted; later it was confirmed by reading the original HTML metadata of dorar.net directly (og:description).
footnotes.19: Imam Ahmad and al-Nasa’i (through Mu‘adh ibn Rifa‘ah ← Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA)); also quoted in Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir. Ibn Kathir called this chain ‘close to the condition of al-Bukhari and Muslim’. In another narration of the same event (Ibn Ishaq, through several unnamed narrators) it is reported that Jibril (AS) came at night wearing a brocade turban and announced Sa‘d (RA)’s death; this part is weak in chain and was not used in the dars.
footnotes.20: Musnad Ahmad 24663 (from ‘A’ishah (RA), with the chain Shu‘bah ← Sa‘d ibn Ibrahim ← Nafi‘ ← an unnamed man ← ‘A’ishah (RA)). The hadith expert Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut called it sahih; it is in Ibn Hibban too. Although the chain has the single step ‘Nafi‘ from an unnamed man’, overall it is considered sahih.

quiz.q: Whom did the Prophet ﷺ send on the stormy night to bring news of the enemy camp?
o: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA)
‘Ali (RA)
‘Umar (RA)
Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA) himself

quiz.q: Why was the storm called ‘only a means’?
o: The same kind of wind destroyed ‘Ad and helped the Muslims
That storm in reality had no real effect at all
Because there is no scientific explanation of the storm
It is merely the language of poets
quiz.e: In the light of Sahih al-Bukhari 4105.

quiz.q: Why did Hudhayfah (RA) not shoot Abu Sufyan with the arrow?
o: The Prophet’s ﷺ instruction was not to startle them
No arrow at all remained in the quiver then
He feared missing the target
He could not recognise Abu Sufyan in the dark

quiz.q: What can be learned about the mindset in times of danger from the storm incident?
o: No danger ever passes by itself
The power of nature is the greatest
Allah’s help can come even by unexpected paths
Human effort is really meaningless

quiz.q: Why did the Prophet ﷺ blame no one over the two understandings about the ‘Asr prayer?
o: The matter was not important to him at all
Both understandings were sincere and reasonable
He could not judge for lack of time
He only wanted to keep everyone happy

quiz.q: What can be applied from accepting two honest understandings of the same command?
o: All differences are really wrong, only one correct view should exist
The leader’s command should be kept unclear
If a command is not understood, it is better to ignore it
One can be tolerant of any difference of opinion held with an honest intention

quiz.q: How many proposals did Ka‘b ibn Asad give his community?
o: Two
Three
Four
Five

quiz.q: What did Abu Lubabah (RA) signal with his hand?
o: Toward the sky, a hint of mercy
Toward the fortress, a hint of surrender
Toward the throat, a hint of killing
Toward the sword, a hint of war

quiz.q: Why is it important that Sa‘d’s judgment matched the law of the Torah?
o: Banu Qurayzah were especially pleased with this judgment
It was merely a coincidental match
It proves he did not show partiality for old alliances
The Islamic ruling was changed by it

quiz.q: Why did Abu Lubabah (RA) tie himself to the pillar of the mosque?
o: Because the Prophet ﷺ himself had given him this punishment
Regretting, taking his own signal as betrayal
Because the people of Banu Qurayzah had forcibly kept him captive
Because he had been wounded in the war

quiz.q: What can be learned about justice from Sa‘d’s impartial judgment?
o: Justice should not be swayed by old relationships
A judge will always rule in favour of his own tribe
One should not judge while wounded
The judgment on an enemy must always be the harshest

quiz.q: What can be learned today from Abu Lubabah’s admission of his mistake?
o: When one errs it is better to hide it
Once one has erred there is no way back
On realising a mistake one should admit it with honest courage
Pointing out others’ mistakes is the most important thing
quiz.e: A lesson from Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir.
